Almsdeeds
amz'deeds
n. pl. (deeds of charity; acts of mercy done to the poor)
From alms, Saxon aelmesse, contracted from Greek eleemosune, mercy, pity, from eleos, mercy — and deeds. The compound insists that mercy is something done.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, and it is an epitaph: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” (Act 9:36). Luke could have written that she was known for her kindness. Instead he writes good works and almsdeeds which she did — and then the narrative shows the widows standing around her body holding up the coats and garments she had made. That is what almsdeeds look like in the record: cloth, cut and sewn, for women with no husband to provide. The compound word itself is the doctrine, since mercy in Scripture is never an attitude that stops short of a deed. The angel says as much to Cornelius: “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God” (Act 10:4) — prayers and alms rising together, neither one standing alone. And the Lord fixes the manner: “when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Mat 6:3). Dorcas is the pattern exactly: her almsdeeds were unknown enough that they had to be displayed by weeping widows after she died.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines almsdeed as an act of charity; a charitable gift; and alms as what is given gratuitously for the relief of the poor.

expand to see more

ALMS'DEED, n. amz'deed. An act of charity; a charitable gift.

ALMS, n. amz. [Sax. aelmesse; Gr. eleemosune, from eleos, mercy.]

Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing, otherwise called charity.

A pious man is to be known by his alms-deeds.

This woman was full of good works and alms-deeds which she did. Acts 9.

Key Scripture

Acts 9:36 — "Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did."

Acts 10:4 — "And when he looked on him, he was afraid, and said, What is it, Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God."

Matthew 6:3 — "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:"

James 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Modern Corruption

Mercy has been professionalized and publicized — delegated to institutions and reported for credit — which removes both the deed and the secrecy.

expand to see more

Matthew 6:3 forbids the left hand knowing what the right hand does, and the modern charitable economy is built on the opposite principle: the giving is announced, branded, and counted, because visibility raises more. The corruption is not that organized relief is wrong — the Jerusalem collection was organized, audited, and carried by approved men. It is that the individual Christian's own hands have largely been retired from the work. Dorcas made the coats herself. A cheque discharges a bill; it does not by itself produce the thing Luke thought worth an epitaph.

There is also a doctrinal caution. Acts 10:4 says Cornelius's prayers and alms came up as a memorial before God, and Rome has read such texts as evidence that alms merit favour — the treasury of merit rests on this instinct. But Cornelius was not saved by his alms; the angel's next instruction is to send for Peter, who must tell him words whereby he shall be saved. God noticed his mercy and answered it by sending him the gospel. Almsdeeds are the fruit of faith and the evidence of pure religion (Jas 1:27); they have never been its purchase price.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eleemosune (G1654), alms, mercy shown; eleos (G1656), mercy; agathon ergon (G18, G2041), good works; Saxon aelmesse.

expand to see more

Greek eleemosunon hon epoiei (G1654) — almsdeeds which she did; Acts 9:36, with the relative clause insisting on the doing.

Greek eleos (G1656) — mercy; the root of eleemosune, and of the English alms by long contraction.

Greek mnemosunon (G3422) — a memorial; Acts 10:4, the sacrificial word for the portion that ascends.

Greek Dorkas (G1393) — a gazelle; the Greek rendering of the Aramaic Tabitha.

Saxon aelmesse — alms; Webster's root, worn down from the Greek across a thousand years.

Usage

"“Full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” — and the widows held up the coats."

"“Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial” — the two ascend together."

"“Let not thy left hand know” — which is why Dorcas needed weeping widows to publish hers."
